title: Rejoining UNIDO: Why Now?
label: 15 September 2026 · UNIDO evidence
summary: The committee questioned Matt Toombs about why the UK should rejoin UNIDO after leaving in 2012, what reforms have occurred, and how membership would benefit UK businesses and developing countries. Toombs argued the context has changed, the UK already has deep programme relationships, and that rejoining would give influence and access to growing green industrial markets, with a review planned for 2029.

chapters.title: Why rejoin UNIDO now?
chapters.takeaway: The UK wants to rejoin UNIDO because the world has changed and the UK already has a deep programme relationship, making membership more valuable for influence and trade.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Why should we actually rejoin UNIDO? We have a good relationship, we don't have to get involved in the politics, and it's a successful delivery agent. Also, what genuine reforms justify reversing our decision to leave 15 years ago?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: Thanks for having me. The context now is very different from 2012, and our relationship with UNIDO has changed too. We've been working closely with them through COP26, on green public procurement with India, and on big programmes like the £125 million Accelerate-to-Demonstrate. So the value of rejoining is much larger now—it gives us influence and opens access for British business.

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: On reforms: UNIDO is smaller and more efficient than when we left. It has an independent evaluation unit, publishes effectiveness data, and is much more transparent. That's why we think it's time to move.

chapters.title: Other countries' positions
chapters.takeaway: Some countries that left might return, but the UK is building on five years of engagement rather than starting from scratch.

turns.speaker: Baroness Anelay of St Johns
turns.text: You've given substance to how the context has changed. What about other countries that left? Have you discussed with them whether they might return? If not, why not, given the benefits you mention?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: We're talking to like-minded countries, but I won't speak for them. Many industrialised countries like Japan, Italy, Germany and the EU remain in UNIDO, so we wouldn't be an exception. This is a path we've been on for at least five years, strengthening our relationship and seeing where the benefits are.

turns.speaker: Baroness Anelay of St Johns
turns.text: But some countries still think it's not worth joining. Do you think others might rejoin?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: The short answer is yes. Next week at the UN General Assembly and Climate Week NYC, green industrialisation will be discussed. It's a priority for the Turkish COP31 and Ethiopian COP32 presidencies. We've built confidence through programmes, and we'd expect other countries to take a similar route.

chapters.title: UNIDO and climate finance
chapters.takeaway: Toombs argues that UNIDO membership helps scale up climate finance impact, using the Brazil example where £15m UK investment unlocked £250m and could raise £2bn private finance.

turns.speaker: Lord Boateng
turns.text: Japan, Italy and Germany have always been strong on industrial policy and their economies thrived. But we've spent billions on aid with insufficient impact, and now we're cutting our development budget. How will UNIDO membership help people facing climate and water emergencies, especially when less than 3% of global climate finance goes to water and sanitation?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: I agree we must support those who need it most. Our international climate finance is smaller, so we have to prioritise and make money go further. UNIDO membership helps us scale up—like in Brazil, where £15m of UK investment alongside Brazil's industrial development led to £250m of wider international finance and is expected to raise £2bn in private finance. That creates jobs and changes livelihoods.

turns.speaker: Lord Boateng
turns.text: That's good, but how does UNIDO membership specifically assist people who can't access green climate finance?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: By being a member, we can help transform outcomes for vulnerable communities and countries, not just fund small projects. The Brazil example shows how a relatively small UK investment can unlock much larger sums and have real impact on the ground.

chapters.title: Reforming climate finance access and ODA
chapters.takeaway: Both witnesses agree that accessing climate finance is too complicated and that ODA needs to be fit for purpose, with more private sector involvement.

turns.speaker: Baroness Verma
turns.text: Is it time to revisit how climate finance is accessed? It's complicated, takes too long, and those who need it most can't get it. And should we look at whether ODA is fit for purpose for this century?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: Access to finance is a real challenge, and the UK is working with the Green Climate Fund and others to speed it up. It's a wider ODA issue—with smaller budgets, we need to use money where it can have the greatest effect and mobilise wider finance. That's increasingly important.

turns.speaker: Baroness Verma
turns.text: Are you restricted by ODA rules when working with private companies? To get private investment, ODA must be easier for businesses to navigate.

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: Absolutely. Strong connection between private finance and publicly financed activities is critical. We have examples with UNIDO involving UK businesses—green tea in Kenya, green steel in South Africa. The private sector must be fully part of the solution.

chapters.title: Engagement with other countries
chapters.takeaway: The UK talks to Australia and New Zealand about industrial development and COP, but won't comment on their UNIDO membership positions; the US has withdrawn from many agencies.

turns.speaker: Baroness Lawlor
turns.text: What about the US, Australia and New Zealand? Have you engaged with them? Are they likely to go back?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: I won't speak to individual countries' positions. The US's broader position on climate change is well known, and it has withdrawn from a number of agencies and reduced funding. But we work with Australia and New Zealand closely, and Australia has taken on the COP presidency alongside Turkey, so we're talking to them about industrial development.

turns.speaker: Baroness Lawlor
turns.text: Do you know if Australia is going back?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: I wouldn't want to comment on its specific relationship with UNIDO.

chapters.title: Preventing backsliding and reviewing membership
chapters.takeaway: Toombs says membership gives the UK more levers to prevent UNIDO slipping backwards, and there will be a UK review in 2029 to check if benefits are being achieved.

turns.speaker: Lord Hannay of Chiswick
turns.text: How do we ensure UNIDO doesn't slip backwards, like the FAO did? And how do we stop it turf-fighting with other UN organisations?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: We wouldn't assume it won't slip. Being a member gives us greater engagement and oversight, so we have stronger levers if things go wrong. On turf fighting, the UN80 reforms are important—many agencies are streamlining. Being part of it helps ensure it's run effectively.

turns.speaker: Lord Hannay of Chiswick
turns.text: Have you established a fixed-term review, say after five years, to see if UNIDO is still reforming? Will you come back to this committee?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: We plan to review whether we're achieving the benefits of rejoining in 2029, linked to our funding agreement. It's a UK review of our decision, not a UNIDO review.

turns.speaker: Lord Hannay of Chiswick
turns.text: If Parliament is involved in that review, would it help your hand in UNIDO governance?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: Our intention is to make rejoining a positive, sustained move. But it's right to review whether we're achieving the benefits we've set out in three years.
